problem.statement: WPF UserControls instantiated off-screen (e.g. in a Windows Service for headless rendering) can be leaked by an internal focus-handler delegate that survives explicit Dispose() calls, and developers have no reliable way to diagnose or force full teardown.

persona.primary: .NET/WPF developer running WPF controls headlessly in a server-side service or batch process

context.situation: A developer renders images from a custom WPF UserControl on a background STA thread inside a Windows Service, and a memory profiler shows each instance leaking via what appears to be an internal focus-handler delegate even though the control itself never subscribed to any events.

current_workarounds: Calling ctrl.Dispose() after rendering, which the developer confirms does not resolve the leak
existing_substitutes: .Net Memory Profiler (used to detect the leak, not to fix it)

possible_wedges.offer: A focused leak-diagnosis utility that attaches to a running .NET process, walks GC roots for WPF UserControl instances, and pinpoints internal delegate/event chains (e.g. FocusManager, InputManager) keeping them alive.

A Roslyn/analyzer plugin for legacy WPF audit tooling that flags code patterns known to cause headless/off-thread WPF control leaks (e.g. UserControl created without a HwndSource, missing explicit focus/input manager cleanup).
A paid deep-dive audit where a WPF memory expert reviews a specific leaking control and profiler dump and delivers a concrete fix, targeted at teams doing headless WPF rendering.

risks: Single evidence item from one forum post; no corroborating reports of this exact leak pattern
Commercial intent signal is very low (0.1) and no willingness-to-pay is expressed
No named competing tools or substitutes beyond the profiler already used to detect (not fix) the issue
Scenario is a niche edge case (headless/off-UI-thread WPF rendering in a service) rather than mainstream WPF app usage, which may limit addressable market
Unclear whether the root cause is a general WPF framework quirk or specific to this developer's control, which affects how broadly a fix/tool would generalize

cheapest_experiment.hypothesis: WPF/.NET developers doing headless UserControl rendering in services would engage with a free, concrete root-cause explanation and fix for this exact focus-handler leak, indicating latent demand for a diagnostic tool or paid audit.
cheapest_experiment.input: A detailed, technically accurate answer/blog post explaining the FocusManager/InputManager delegate root cause and a working fix for the reported StackOverflow-style question, with a link to a simple free diagnostic checklist or waitlist for a deeper tool.
cheapest_experiment.output: Upvotes, accepted-answer status, comments, and click-through/signup rate on the linked checklist or waitlist.
cheapest_experiment.commitment_event: A reader clicks through to join a waitlist or requests a paid deep-dive review of their own leak.
cheapest_experiment.success_threshold: At least 5-10 independent developers engage (upvote/comment/click) within a few weeks, with at least 1-2 waitlist signups or paid inquiries, suggesting the pattern recurs beyond one report.
cheapest_experiment.failure_threshold: Answer/post gets essentially no engagement (no independent confirmations of the same leak pattern) and zero signups after a few weeks, suggesting the issue is too rare to build around.
